entries.title: Learning Fair Representations
entries.name: Learning Fair Representations
entries.definition: A prototype-based representation-learning algorithm that jointly balances reconstruction, supervised prediction and differences between group-average prototype assignment probabilities.
entries.mechanism: Map an individual to softmax probabilities over learned prototypes using negative distances. Optimize prototype locations and bounded prototype label probabilities with a weighted sum of squared reconstruction loss, predictive cross-entropy and absolute differences of mean assignment probabilities between two protected groups. The paper also learns feature-distance weights separately by group and uses L-BFGS for its optimization.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.3, equations (1)–(12), PDF pp. 2–4; Section 4.1, PDF p. 6 for optimization
entries.identity_notes: The named LFR algorithm learns a prototype representation and a prediction rule. It is distinct from the general aim of learning fair representations, the finite-population FairnessLP formulation, and the later Variational Fair Autoencoder. The learned metric variant does not make it identical to AIO MetricLearning, which denotes a deep neural network in this pin.
limitations: Fairness, reconstruction and predictive utility are weighted objectives; finite training and a nonzero penalty weight do not guarantee exact population parity.

Equal group means of assignment probabilities do not imply equality of the distributions of the full assignment-probability vectors. Arbitrary nonlinear downstream processing or thresholding requires a separate fairness assessment.
The method encourages local similarity; it does not certify the full supplied-metric pairwise Lipschitz criterion for every pair of individuals.
The group-specific distance variant uses group membership for its mapping. Out-of-sample representation availability is not a proof of out-of-sample fairness.
entries.mapping_rationale: Learns a representation and prediction rule for classification. The algorithm is related to the classification task; the pin’s RepresentationLearning and MetricLearning classes specifically describe deep neural networks and are not asserted as exact or broad identities for this prototype method.

additional_evidence.title: The Variational Fair Autoencoder
additional_evidence.claim: Louizos and colleagues identify a higher-order-distribution limitation of matching average LFR assignment probabilities: groups can have the same average assignment while the distribution of those probability values differs. This concerns the exposed probability-vector representation, not a refutation of parity of an exactly matched sampled prototype index.
additional_evidence.locator: Related Work, Section 4, PDF pp. 8–9, paragraph beginning with the comparison to Zemel et al.

entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes fair classification through a learned intermediate prototype representation, balancing information retention and group obfuscation. Full-method inspection narrows its fairness claim to an optimized mean-assignment penalty and explicitly scoped prediction behavior.

entries.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
entries.name: Exponentiated-gradient reduction for fair classification
entries.definition: A cost-sensitive classification reduction that alternates classifier best responses with exponentiated-gradient updates of bounded Lagrange multipliers to approximate an error–fairness saddle point and return a randomized classifier mixture.
entries.mechanism: Express fairness as linear inequalities on conditional prediction moments whose conditioning events do not depend on the classifier. Given multiplier values, call a cost-sensitive classification oracle with modified per-example label costs. Update multipliers from constraint violations using exponentiated gradient, average the classifiers and multipliers, and stop when the computed saddle-point gap reaches the chosen tolerance.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.2 and 3.1–3.3, equations (1)–(6), Algorithm 1, BESTh/BESTlambda constructions, Theorems 1–3, PDF pp. 2–6
entries.identity_notes: This is Algorithm 1 of Agarwal et al., not generic exponentiated-gradient optimization. It returns a distribution over classifiers and is distinct from the paper’s deterministic-candidate grid-search reduction and from postprocessing a fixed classifier.
limitations: The optimization analysis assumes a cost-sensitive best-response oracle; heuristic base learners need not realize the exact oracle guarantees.
Bounds retain optimization tolerance, the multiplier-norm cap and statistical error, including dependence on the number of observations in each conditioning event.
The constraint representation excludes conditioning events that depend on the learned predictor; the paper identifies predictive parity and calibration as outside this formulation.

Protected attributes are required for training constraints. No separate protected-attribute argument is needed at prediction time only when the chosen feature vector and base classifier do not require it.
entries.mapping_rationale: Trains binary classifiers under conditional-moment constraints. The reduction is a learning algorithm related to the binary classification task, not an equivalent task or ontology subclass assertion.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Reduces binary fair classification to cost-sensitive learning. Full reading separates an exponentiated-gradient randomized mixture from deterministic candidates obtained by grid search, retaining oracle, moment-constraint and finite-sample assumptions.

entries.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
entries.name: Grid-search reduction for fair classification
entries.definition: A fairness-aware classification reduction that evaluates cost-sensitive classifier best responses over a grid of Lagrange-multiplier-derived costs and selects a deterministic candidate with a desired empirical accuracy–fairness tradeoff.
entries.mechanism: Use the same linear conditional-moment constraint formulation and per-example cost-sensitive oracle as the exponentiated-gradient reduction, but enumerate candidate multiplier values or equivalent cost adjustments. For binary protected groups the paper reduces demographic-parity search to one adjustment dimension and equalized-odds search to two, then compares candidate classifiers to select the desired tradeoff.
entries.locator: Section 3.2 BESTh construction, PDF pp. 4–5; Section 3.4, Examples 7–8, PDF pp. 6–7
entries.identity_notes: The paper’s Section 3.4 grid search is a separate reduction producing deterministic candidates. It shares a cost-sensitive oracle with the randomized exponentiated-gradient reduction but does not inherit that procedure’s mixture or saddle-point stopping rule. It is not generic hyperparameter grid search or the bivariate causal-sensitivity grid procedure.
limitations: A finite grid and heuristic cost-sensitive learner do not guarantee a globally optimal fair deterministic classifier.
The paper explicitly allows lower accuracy or constraint violation when choosing a deterministic candidate; the randomized-mixture guarantees should not be transferred automatically.
Grid search is intended for small numbers of effective constraint dimensions and scales poorly as that dimension grows.
Fairness is assessed under the specified empirical constraints and sampling context; evaluation on unseen or shifted data is separate.
entries.mapping_rationale: Constructs binary classification candidates using fairness-dependent costs. This relates the reduction to its task without equating algorithm and task.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Reduces binary fair classification to cost-sensitive learning. Full reading separates an exponentiated-gradient randomized mixture from deterministic candidates obtained by grid search, retaining oracle, moment-constraint and finite-sample assumptions.

entries.title: The Variational Fair Autoencoder
entries.name: Variational Fair Autoencoder
entries.definition: A variational autoencoder architecture for learning representations with reduced sensitive or nuisance information, combining sensitive-variable-conditioned inference and generation with an MMD penalty on group-conditional aggregated latent distributions and a semi-supervised predictive component.
entries.mechanism: Use neural inference and generative models conditioned on the observed sensitive variable, with latent structure separating that variable from the representation in the generative model. In the semi-supervised construction, introduce a second latent layer and label variable and jointly train the inference, reconstruction and predictive components. Penalize differences between aggregated latent distributions across sensitive groups with maximum mean discrepancy, approximated using random Fourier features in the reported implementation.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.4, Figures 1–2 and equations (1)–(10), PDF pp. 2–4; Section 3.2, PDF pp. 5–6 for prediction sampling
entries.identity_notes: VFAE denotes the MMD-regularized semi-supervised variational architecture introduced by Louizos et al. It is distinct from the paper’s unregularized VAE baseline, prototype-based LFR, ordinary autoencoding and the model-dependent FAIRLEARNING algorithm. Prior independence and aggregated-posterior matching do not establish causal counterfactual fairness.
limitations: Independence in the generative prior does not alone ensure independence of inferred representations; the MMD regularizer addresses remaining group dependence.
Finite data, optimization, kernel choice and random-feature approximation limit how strongly matching can be claimed; no exact population independence or universal fairness guarantee is asserted.
The encoder conditions on the sensitive variable. Semi-supervised here allows missing task labels, not arbitrary absence of sensitive-attribute information.

The paper reports sampling the inferred latent representation for prediction rather than replacing it by its mean. Numerical objective-sign and bandwidth conventions are not certified by this conceptual record.
entries.mapping_rationale: Uses variational autoencoding with additional sensitive-variable conditioning, a supervised component and MMD regularization. Because the pinned target definition specifies unsupervised learning, this mapping records the architectural relationship without asserting an unqualified subclass relation.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes nuisance-invariant variational representations with MMD regularization. Full reading distinguishes prior independence from aggregate posterior matching, sensitive-variable availability from label availability, and intended invariance from a universal causal fairness guarantee.

entries.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
entries.name: Adversarial debiasing (Zhang et al.)
entries.definition: An adversarial learning algorithm that trains a task predictor alongside a protected-attribute adversary, modifying the predictor gradient with a projection term and an opposing adversary-loss term to target a selected statistical fairness condition.
entries.mechanism: Train the adversary to predict the protected attribute from differentiable predictor outputs, optionally also using true labels for equalized odds or a label-restricted training subset for equal opportunity. For the predictor, remove the component of its task-loss gradient along the adversary-loss gradient and subtract a weighted adversary-loss gradient from the update gradient. The source defines a zero projection when the adversary gradient is zero.
entries.locator: Section 3 equation (1), PDF pp. 2–3; Section 5 Propositions 1–3 and footnote 4, PDF pp. 3–4; Section 8, PDF p. 6
entries.identity_notes: This record isolates Zhang, Lemoine and Mitchell’s projection-based method. It is not the whole family of adversarial fairness approaches, a generative adversarial network, or generic gradient reversal. Different adversary inputs target different fairness constraints rather than defining synonyms for those criteria.
limitations: The source’s convergence argument assumes convexity/concavity, differentiability and convergence; it explicitly notes that the convexity/concavity assumptions usually fail for neural networks.

Turning adversarial indistinguishability into a population fairness condition requires a sufficiently expressive and well-optimized adversary. Failure of a restricted adversary to detect dependence is not proof of general independence.
Training can be unstable and is sensitive to optimization settings and loss weighting; the method does not guarantee convergence or exact finite-sample fairness.
The projection describes an ideal gradient construction. This record does not certify every finite-step or adaptive-optimizer implementation, and omits numerical benchmark claims.
entries.mapping_rationale: Modifies gradient-based supervised predictive training for classification or regression. The algorithm relates to the learning paradigm and is not mapped as a generative model merely because it uses an adversary.

additional_evidence.title: FR-Train: A Mutual Information-Based Approach to Fair and Robust Training
additional_evidence.claim: The FR-Train authors explicitly omit the Zhang et al. projection term, reporting that it worsened training stability in their experiments. This is a setting-dependent design observation, not evidence that projection-based adversarial debiasing always fails.
additional_evidence.locator: Section 3.1, PDF p. 4, paragraph discussing Adversarial Debiasing immediately before Section 3.2

source_caveats.observation: The probability vector exposed to downstream models is distinguished from a sampled categorical prototype. Equal means imply neither identical probability-vector distributions nor arbitrary-threshold parity. No paper’s broad informal fairness claim is promoted to an unconditional record guarantee.

Exact cost-sensitive oracle assumptions, randomized versus deterministic outputs, multiplier caps, sample sizes and classifier-independent conditioning events are retained. Grid search does not inherit the mixture’s guarantee.

The record does not reproduce numerical objective-sign or random-feature bandwidth conventions as executable formulas. Equation 5’s displayed supervised negative-log term and maximization prose require implementation-level reconciliation; the apparent kernel-bandwidth convention also remains unverified. Dataset prose differs from figure descriptions and is not used for numerical or demographic benchmark claims.

An attempted plausible author-lab URL, https://github.com/AMLab-Amsterdam/VFAE, returned 404. Search located third-party lists but did not establish an authoritative versioned implementation; no code inspection is claimed.

The original paper explicitly notes strong theoretical assumptions and convergence difficulty. The follow-up authors’ projection-stability observation is retained as setting-dependent, without a numerical or universal superiority claim.

limitations: All five concepts remain DRAFT and scientific review is author self-review, not independent approval.
Primary methods and bounded follow-up limitations were inspected; code, quantitative benchmarks and full proof correctness were not reproduced.
Known source ambiguities are retained, not silently converted to implementation guidance.
